references.authors: Kashtan YS, Nicholson M, Finnegan C, et al.
references.title: Gas and Propane Combustion from Stoves Emits Benzene and Increases Indoor Air Pollution.
references.finding: Gas and propane burners and ovens emitted 2.8-6.5 ug benzene per minute, 10-25 times more than electric coil or radiant stoves; induction and the food itself emitted none, and benzene spread to bedrooms.

references.authors: Li W, Goodman JE, Long C
references.title: Population attributable fraction of gas cooking and childhood asthma: What was missed?
references.finding: Gradient consultancy commentary, funded by the American Gas Association, arguing that the 12.7% population attributable fraction for gas cooking and childhood asthma is not valid.

references.authors: Li W, Long C, Fan T, et al.
references.title: Gas cooking and respiratory outcomes in children: A systematic review.
references.finding: Systematic review by Gradient (a consultancy that has worked for gas-industry clients) judged most gas cooking-asthma studies cross-sectional and biased, with cohort studies largely null, and concluded causal inference is not supported.

references.authors: Lin W, Brunekreef B, Gehring U
references.title: Meta-analysis of the effects of indoor nitrogen dioxide and gas cooking on asthma and wheeze in children.
references.finding: Gas cooking was associated with childhood asthma (OR 1.32, 95% CI 1.18-1.48) and indoor NO2 with current wheeze (OR 1.15 per 15 ppb); no evidence of publication bias.

references.authors: Sehgal AR, Schuellerman P, Dolata J, et al.
references.title: Asthma Control Before and After Changing Gas Stoves to Electric Stoves.
references.finding: Uncontrolled before-after study: after gas stoves were replaced with electric ones, indoor NO2 fell from 21.0 to 6.3 ppb and Asthma Control Questionnaire scores improved from 2.6 to 1.5 within 2-3 months.

references.authors: Paulin LM, Diette GB, Scott M, et al.
references.title: Home interventions are effective at decreasing indoor nitrogen dioxide concentrations.
references.finding: Replacing the gas stove with electric cut median kitchen NO2 by 51% at 3 months; HEPA-plus-carbon purifiers cut it 27% immediately (20% at 3 months); a new range hood did not significantly lower NO2.

references.authors: Pilotto LS, Nitschke M, Smith BJ, et al.
references.title: Randomized controlled trial of unflued gas heater replacement on respiratory health of asthmatic schoolchildren.
references.finding: Replacing unflued gas heaters in schools lowered classroom NO2 (15.5 vs 47.0 ppb) and cut daytime and night-time asthma symptoms (RR about 0.3-0.45), without changing lung function.

references.authors: Howden-Chapman P, Pierse N, Nicholls S, et al.
references.title: Effects of improved home heating on asthma in community dwelling children: randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: Installing non-polluting, more effective heaters lowered NO2 and reduced school absence, doctor visits, sleep disturbed by wheezing and night cough, but did not significantly improve lung function.

references.authors: Barregard L, Sällsten G, Andersson L, et al.
references.title: Experimental exposure to wood smoke: effects on airway inflammation and oxidative stress.
references.finding: Four hours of wood smoke at 240-280 ug/m3 raised airway markers of inflammation and oxidative stress (exhaled breath MDA, alveolar NO) in a chamber.

references.authors: Forchhammer L, Møller P, Riddervold IS, et al.
references.title: Controlled human wood smoke exposure: oxidative stress, inflammation and microvascular function.
references.finding: Three hours of wood smoke at 220 or 354 ug/m3 did not change oxidatively damaged DNA, inflammatory markers or microvascular function.

references.authors: Walker ES, Semmens EO, Belcourt A, et al.
references.title: Efficacy of Air Filtration and Education Interventions on Indoor Fine Particulate Matter and Child Lower Respiratory Tract Infections among Rural U.S. Homes Heated with Wood Stoves: Results from the KidsAIR Randomized Trial.
references.finding: In wood-stove-heated homes, portable air filtration or education did not reduce child lower respiratory tract infections or measured indoor PM2.5 versus control, though LRTI odds rose 1.45-fold per 25 ug/m3 PM2.5.

references.authors: Ward TJ, Semmens EO, Weiler E, et al.
references.title: Efficacy of interventions targeting household air pollution from residential wood stoves.
references.finding: Air filtration units cut indoor PM2.5 by 63% vs placebo filters, while wood-stove changeouts did not significantly lower PM2.5; compliance was a problem.

references.authors: Clasen TF, Chang HH, Thompson LM, et al.
references.title: Liquefied Petroleum Gas or Biomass for Cooking and Effects on Birth Weight.
references.finding: A free LPG stove and fuel cut personal PM2.5 from 70.7 to 23.9 ug/m3 but did not change birth weight (adjusted difference 19.6 g, 95% CI -10.1 to 49.2).

references.authors: McCollum ED, McCracken JP, Kirby MA, et al.
references.title: Liquefied Petroleum Gas or Biomass Cooking and Severe Infant Pneumonia.

references.authors: Mortimer K, Ndamala CB, Naunje AW, et al.
references.title: A cleaner burning biomass-fuelled cookstove intervention to prevent pneumonia in children under 5 years old in rural Malawi (the Cooking and Pneumonia Study): a cluster randomised controlled trial.
references.finding: Cleaner-burning biomass cookstoves did not reduce pneumonia in children under 5 (IRR 1.01).

references.authors: Chen R, Zhao A, Chen H, et al.
references.title: Cardiopulmonary benefits of reducing indoor particles of outdoor origin: a randomized, double-blind crossover trial of air purifiers.
references.finding: Forty-eight hours of real vs sham air purification cut indoor PM2.5 by 57% and lowered blood pressure and several inflammatory and coagulation markers.

references.authors: Wang Y, Zhao Y, Xue L, et al.
references.title: Effects of air purification of indoor PM(2.5) on the cardiorespiratory biomarkers in young healthy adults.
references.finding: A week of HEPA purification lowered indoor PM2.5 and improved some cardiorespiratory biomarkers including urinary 8-isoprostane.

references.authors: Walzer D, Gordon T, Thorpe L, et al.
references.title: Effects of Home Particulate Air Filtration on Blood Pressure: A Systematic Review.
references.finding: Home HEPA filtration over a median 13.5 days lowered systolic BP by about 4 mmHg (-3.94, 95% CI -7.00 to -0.89) but not diastolic BP.

references.authors: Xia X, Chan KH, Lam KBH, et al.
references.title: Effectiveness of indoor air purification intervention in improving cardiovascular health: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.
references.finding: Purifiers lowered systolic BP by 2.28 mmHg with no significant change in CRP or diastolic BP; certainty of evidence was very low, discouraging unsubstantiated claims.

references.authors: Wittkopp S, Walzer D, Thorpe L, et al.
references.title: Portable air cleaner use and biomarkers of inflammation: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Portable air cleaners cut PM2.5 by 61.5% and were associated with 7% lower CRP and 13% lower IL-6, with no TNF-alpha change.

references.authors: Barn P, Gombojav E, Ochir C, et al.
references.title: The effect of portable HEPA filter air cleaner use during pregnancy on fetal growth: The UGAAR randomized controlled trial.
references.finding: HEPA cleaners from early pregnancy cut indoor PM2.5 by 29% but did not change birth weight overall (+18 g, 95% CI -84 to 120); +85 g in a subgroup of term births.

references.authors: Morishita M, Adar SD, D'Souza J, et al.
references.title: Effect of Portable Air Filtration Systems on Personal Exposure to Fine Particulate Matter and Blood Pressure Among Residents in a Low-Income Senior Facility: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
references.finding: Three days of portable filtration lowered personal PM2.5 and systolic BP by 3.2 mmHg vs sham; most secondary outcomes did not improve.

references.authors: Brook RD, Song Y, Bard RL, et al.
references.title: Bedroom Air Filtration and Home Blood Pressures of Older Adults Living in a Residential Facility.
references.finding: Four weeks of bedroom HEPA filtration cut bedroom PM2.5 (1.3 vs 8.3 ug/m3) but did not change home systolic BP (127.0 vs 126.5 mmHg).

references.authors: Qiu AY, Brigham EP, Woo H, et al.
references.title: AIRWEIGHS: A Randomized Controlled Trial of Air Cleaners in Normal Weight and Overweight/Obese Children With Asthma.
references.finding: HEPA air cleaners cut indoor PM2.5 by 64% and ultrafine particles by 64% over 12 weeks but did not improve asthma symptom days, lung function or exacerbations.

references.authors: Paradisi R, Vanella S, Barzanti R, et al.
references.title: Effects of indoor air purification by an air cleaning system (Koala technology) on semen parameters in male factor infertility: results of a pilot study.
references.finding: A year of indoor air purification in men with poor semen quality produced no improvement in semen parameters or reproductive hormones.

references.authors: Li Z, Liu Q, Xu Z, et al.
references.title: Association between short-term exposure to ambient particulate air pollution and biomarkers of oxidative stress: A meta-analysis.
references.finding: Short-term PM2.5 was associated with higher MDA (about 1.6% per 10 ug/m3) and other oxidative stress biomarkers.

references.authors: Rubes J, Selevan SG, Evenson DP, et al.
references.title: Episodic air pollution is associated with increased DNA fragmentation in human sperm without other changes in semen quality.
references.n: Young men sampled up to 7 times (Teplice)
references.finding: Periods of high coal-smoke air pollution were associated with more sperm DNA fragmentation without other semen changes.

references.title: Lifestyle-, environmental-, and additional health factors associated with an increased sperm DNA fragmentation: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Air pollution exposure was among factors associated with higher sperm DNA fragmentation (pooled mean difference about 9.7 points).

references.authors: Legro RS, Sauer MV, Mottla GL, et al.
references.title: Effect of air quality on assisted human reproduction.
references.finding: Higher NO2 at the patient's address and IVF lab was associated with lower chance of live birth.

references.title: Elevated levels of nitrous dioxide are associated with lower AMH levels: a real-world analysis.

references.finding: With up to five AMH measurements over 20 years, long-term NO2, ozone, PM10 and PM2.5 were not associated with AMH across the reproductive lifespan.

references.title: Association between exposure to ambient air pollution and semen quality: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Each 10 ug/m3 PM2.5 was associated with about 1% lower total motility and PM10/SO2 with 2-9% lower sperm concentration; PM2.5, NO2 and ozone were not associated with concentration.

references.title: Does outdoor air pollution cause poor semen quality? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.finding: Higher air pollution exposure was associated with lower semen volume, concentration and motility, with very high heterogeneity (I2 about 96-99%).

references.authors: Qian H, Xu Q, Yan W, et al.
references.title: Association between exposure to ambient air pollution and semen quality in adults: a meta-analysis.
references.finding: Air pollution was associated with small reductions in sperm concentration, count and total motility, but not progressive motility.

references.title: Fine particulate matter exposure and sperm DNA fragmentation in US men: a spatial cross-sectional study.
references.finding: Higher PM2.5 during spermatogenesis was associated with higher DNA fragmentation index, non-linearly, and more strongly in lower-SES areas.

references.title: Long term exposure to road traffic noise and air pollution and risk of infertility in men and women: nationwide Danish cohort study.
references.finding: Each 2.9 ug/m3 higher 5-year PM2.5 was associated with 24% higher risk of an infertility diagnosis in men; PM2.5 was not associated with infertility in women.

references.title: Air Pollution and Mortality in the Medicare Population.
references.finding: PM2.5 and ozone were associated with higher mortality even below current US standards, with no evident threshold.

references.authors: Hansen C, Luben TJ, Sacks JD, et al.
references.title: The effect of ambient air pollution on sperm quality.
references.finding: After adjusting for season and temperature, PM2.5 and ozone were not significantly associated with any semen outcome, including DNA integrity.

references.authors: Barnoya J, Glantz SA
references.title: Cardiovascular effects of secondhand smoke: nearly as large as smoking.
references.finding: Review arguing that brief passive smoking produces cardiovascular effects averaging 80-90% of chronic active smoking, explaining a ~30% excess coronary risk.

references.title: Environmental tobacco smoke and tobacco related mortality in a prospective study of Californians, 1960-98.
references.finding: Marriage to a smoker was not associated with coronary death (RR 0.94 men, 1.01 women) or lung cancer; the paper drew an editorial and many critical letters.

references.authors: Davey Smith G
references.title: Effect of passive smoking on health.
references.finding: BMJ editorial accompanying the Enstrom-Kabat cohort on the effect of passive smoking on health.

references.finding: Self-reported secondhand smoke was associated with 22% higher odds of cardiovascular disease (OR 1.22), with dose-response by amount, duration and cotinine.

references.title: Meta-analysis of the association between second-hand smoke exposure and ischaemic heart diseases, COPD and stroke.
references.finding: Secondhand smoke was associated with ischaemic heart disease (RR 1.27), stroke (1.35) and COPD (1.66).

references.finding: Cochrane: legislative smoking bans were followed by reduced cardiovascular admissions, most consistently for acute coronary syndrome.

references.title: Sidestream smoking is equally as damaging as mainstream smoking on IVF outcomes.
references.finding: Sidestream-exposed women had implantation (12.6%) and pregnancy rates (20.0%) as low as active smokers, versus 25.0% and 48.3% in non-exposed women.

references.finding: One hour of talk-mode phone radiation raised ROS and lowered motility and viability in neat semen in vitro, without DNA damage.

audit.claim: Wood smoke at smoky-home levels raised airway oxidative stress in one chamber study but not systemic markers in another, and gas cooking is linked to childhood asthma though the evidence quality is debated (general impact 2, limited).
audit.biases: Gas-cooking studies are mostly cross-sectional with self-reported exposure and residual confounding by income, crowding, damp and smoking [eia-li2023gas]; reviewers critical of the evidence were consultancy- or industry-linked [eia-li2023gas, eia-li2024gas]. Stove-swap evidence is an uncontrolled before-after design open to regression to the mean and seasonal change [eia-sehgal2026]. Chamber studies are small and short [eia-barregard2008, eia-forchhammer2012].
audit.newer_evidence: Randomized cookstove trials in low-income countries are the big update: switching biomass to LPG cut personal PM2.5 from about 71 to 24 ug/m3 yet did not change birth weight (2022) [eia-clasen2022] or severe infant pneumonia (2024) [eia-mccollum2024], and cleaner biomass stoves did not reduce child pneumonia (2017) [eia-mortimer2017]. In rural US wood-stove homes, air filters and education did not reduce child respiratory infections, although infections rose with measured PM2.5 (2022) [eia-walker2022], and wood-stove changeouts did not lower indoor PM2.5 while filters cut it 63% (2017) [eia-ward2017]. On gas: replacing gas with electric stoves lowered NO2 51% in an RCT (2014) [eia-paulin2014] and improved asthma control in an uncontrolled study (2026) [eia-sehgal2026]; gas burners emit benzene (2023) [eia-kashtan2023]; removing unflued gas heaters reduced asthma symptoms in randomized trials [eia-pilotto2004, eia-howdenchapman2008].
audit.bottom_line: Reducing smoke is worthwhile, but partial reductions (still above WHO levels) have not delivered clinical benefit in large trials, and newer stoves alone did not lower indoor particles where filters did.

site_change.note: Fill the empty debate field (gas-asthma: [eia-lin2013] vs [eia-li2023gas, eia-li2024gas]; wood smoke: [eia-barregard2008] vs [eia-forchhammer2012]; clean-cookstove RCTs null [eia-clasen2022, eia-mccollum2024, eia-mortimer2017]). In dose.effective, add that a wood-stove changeout did not lower indoor PM2.5 in a randomized trial while a HEPA filter did [eia-ward2017], and cross-link the new [gas-stoves] factor for NO2/benzene detail.

audit.claim: Sham-controlled crossover trials show HEPA purifiers halve indoor PM2.5 and lower oxidative and inflammatory markers and blood pressure within days (general impact 3, moderate).
audit.biases: Most positive trials are 2-day to 2-week crossovers in young adults in very polluted Chinese cities, measuring surrogate markers with many outcomes tested [eia-chen2015, eia-wang2021]; GRADE certainty for cardiovascular outcomes is very low [eia-xia2021]. Small-study and publication bias are likely in a field of short, small surrogate trials.
audit.newer_evidence: Meta-analyses agree on a small systolic BP fall of about 2-4 mmHg (2020-2021) [eia-walzer2020, eia-xia2021] and 7% lower CRP and 13% lower IL-6 (2022) [eia-wittkopp2022], and a Detroit seniors trial found -3.2 mmHg over 3 days (2018) [eia-morishita2018]. But longer or clinical-outcome trials are mostly null: 4 weeks of bedroom HEPA did not change home BP in older adults (2026) [eia-brook2026]; 12 weeks of HEPA in 164 children with asthma cut PM2.5 64% with no improvement in symptoms or lung function (2025) [eia-qiu2025]; filters did not reduce child respiratory infections in wood-stove homes (2022) [eia-walker2022]; and HEPA cleaners in pregnancy in Ulaanbaatar did not raise birth weight overall (2018) [eia-barn2018]. The only fertility attempt (1 year of purification in 10 infertile men) found no semen improvement [eia-paradisi2009].
audit.bottom_line: Purifiers reliably cut indoor particles and nudge short-term blood pressure and inflammation markers, but trials of weeks to months have not shown clinical benefit outside very polluted settings. Worth using during smoke events, high-pollution periods or with indoor sources, not as a proven health intervention.

site_change.headline: HEPA purifiers cut indoor PM2.5 by roughly half to two-thirds and lower blood pressure by about 2-4 mmHg and some inflammatory markers within days, but longer trials in children with asthma, pregnant women and older adults have mostly found no clinical benefit.
site_change.note: Fill the debate field: positive surrogate meta-analyses [eia-walzer2020, eia-wittkopp2022] vs very-low-certainty grading [eia-xia2021] and null clinical trials [eia-qiu2025, eia-brook2026, eia-walker2022, eia-barn2018]. Note that plain HEPA does not remove NO2 or VOCs; carbon stages help for gas-stove NO2 [eia-paulin2014].

audit.claim: Fine particles raise oxidative markers (about 1.6% higher MDA per 10 ug/m3), high-pollution periods add about 9.7 points of sperm DNA fragmentation, and NO2 is linked to lower AMH and lower IVF live birth (general 3, sperm 2, egg 2).
audit.biases: Exposure is estimated from home address (misclassification); area-level income, smoking and diet confound between-city comparisons [eia-fouks2025]; season and temperature confound semen studies (a US cohort lost its associations after adjusting for them) [eia-hansen2010]; semen meta-analyses have extreme heterogeneity (I2 about 96-99%) [eia-margiana2025]; IVF studies test many pollutants, windows and outcomes [eia-legro2010].
audit.newer_evidence: General: in 61 million Medicare beneficiaries, PM2.5 was associated with mortality even below US standards (2017) [eia-di2017]. Sperm: dose-response meta-analysis found about 1% lower motility per 10 ug/m3 PM2.5 but no PM2.5 effect on concentration (2023) [eia-xu2023]; other meta-analyses report small falls in concentration and motility [eia-qian2022, eia-margiana2025]; in 21,851 US semen samples PM2.5 was associated with higher DNA fragmentation, more in low-SES areas (2025) [eia-fouks2025]; and a nationwide Danish cohort of 526,056 men found 24% higher risk of an infertility diagnosis per 2.9 ug/m3 PM2.5 (2024) [eia-sorensen2024]. Egg: the same Danish cohort found no PM2.5-infertility link in 377,850 women [eia-sorensen2024]; a 20-year Dutch cohort with up to five AMH measurements found no association with NO2 or particles (2025) [eia-zou2025], against the earlier cross-sectional AMH finding [eia-lamarca2020]; men's exposure did not clearly affect IVF live birth (2026) [eia-russo2026].
audit.bottom_line: The general and male-fertility claims hold and the male side is stronger than when written (nationwide cohort data). The egg-side claims are weaker: the best longitudinal AMH study and the Danish female cohort are null, leaving IVF associations from a few clinic cohorts.

site_change.note: Downgrade egg impact to 1 (limited) citing [eia-zou2025, eia-sorensen2024]; add the Danish male infertility result [eia-sorensen2024] and the 2025 US DFI study [eia-fouks2025] to the sperm entry; mention season/temperature confounding [eia-hansen2010]. The sperm and egg entries carry impact.general 4 while the main entry says 3; harmonise to 3. Fill the empty debate fields.

audit.claim: Secondhand smoke raises coronary heart disease risk about 30% and brief exposures produce vascular and oxidative effects averaging 80-90% of active smoking (general 3, sperm 1, egg 2; moderate).
audit.biases: Exposure is usually self-reported spousal or household smoking, which misclassifies exposure in both directions; a cohort using spousal smoking found no association [eia-enstrom2003] and drew a BMJ editorial and many critical letters [eia-daveysmith2003]. The 80-90% figure comes from a narrative review of mechanistic studies, not a pooled estimate [eia-barnoya2005]. The egg claim rests on a small retrospective IVF series [eia-neal2005].
audit.newer_evidence: Newer meta-analyses put the cardiovascular excess at about 22-27%: OR 1.22 for CVD with a dose-response by cotinine and duration (2020) [eia-zhang2020shs] and RR 1.27 for ischaemic heart disease, 1.35 stroke and 1.66 COPD (2015) [eia-fischer2015]. Smoking-ban studies show fewer acute coronary admissions [eia-meyers2009, eia-frazer2016]. One small study found no difference in 8-isoprostane or oxidized LDL with modest exposure [eia-sitihajar2018]. No new controlled data on sperm or egg outcomes were found.
audit.bottom_line: The cardiovascular harm holds, at a slightly smaller size (about 20-27% rather than 30%). The fertility scopes rest on very little direct evidence and should be graded limited.

site_change.headline: Secondhand smoke raises heart disease risk by roughly 20-30% with a dose-response, and even 30 minutes impairs coronary blood flow in healthy non-smokers.
site_change.note: Set evidence_by_scope for sperm and egg to limited (egg rests on a retrospective 40-woman exposed group [eia-neal2005]); soften "80-90% of active smoking" to a quoted review estimate [eia-barnoya2005]; fill the debate field with [eia-enstrom2003, eia-daveysmith2003] vs [eia-zhang2020shs, eia-fischer2015].

audit.claim: Phone radiation raises ROS in semen in a dish, but human studies are inconsistent with no dose-response; keep the phone out of the front trouser pocket as a low-cost precaution (sperm impact 1, limited).
audit.biases: Self-reported phone use; heavy users differ in sedentary time, BMI and socioeconomic factors; in vitro studies expose neat semen at close range in conditions unlike pocket carriage [eia-agarwal2009]. Risk of bias for exposure assessment was high in most studies in the WHO reviews [eia-cordelli2024, eia-kenny2024].
audit.newer_evidence: The WHO-commissioned reviews (2024) found very uncertain evidence for any effect of duration of phone use on human semen and little or no effect of front-pocket carriage on semen or time to pregnancy [eia-kenny2024]; animal data suggested lower pregnancy rate (moderate certainty) and sperm count (low certainty), and in vitro human sperm data showed only a small effect on vitality and none on DNA (very low certainty) [eia-cordelli2024]. In 2,886 Swiss young men (2023), frequent use was linked to lower concentration and count, an association that faded over 2005-2018 as phones changed, with no pocket effect [eia-rahban2023]. Critics argue the WHO reviews cannot establish safety [eia-melnick2025].
audit.bottom_line: The evidence remains weak and uncertain. Keeping the phone out of a front pocket is harmless but not supported by human data.

site_change.note: In dose.effective, state that front-pocket carriage showed little or no effect in human studies [eia-kenny2024, eia-rahban2023], keeping the advice only as optional precaution. Fill the debate field: [eia-kim2021, eia-rahban2023] vs [eia-kenny2024, eia-liu2014]; WHO review methods contested [eia-melnick2025].
